name: unfold-anamorphism
intent: Generate a recursive or potentially unbounded structure from a single seed value by repeatedly applying a step function that emits one layer and returns the next seed, so producers of recursive data become total, independently testable coalgebras instead of ad-hoc loops with allocations scattered through them.
problem: Code that builds a recursive structure - a list, tree, stream, state graph or syntax tree - from an initial value and a per-step rule ends up as a hand-written loop that tangles three separate concerns: deciding when to stop, producing exactly one layer, and assembling the layers into the result. The same recursion is re-derived at every producer, the stop condition drifts between call sites, and demand-driven, infinite or partially forced generation cannot be expressed at all.
context: Applies when the data is defined by a state and a one-step rule rather than by an existing collection: recursive or coinductive types (lists, streams, trees, graphs, abstract syntax), structures that are too large or endless to materialise, and generators whose consumers decide how much to force. It is also the natural producer when the result is immediately consumed by a fold, because the pair fuses into a single traversal.
benefits: One total step function captures the producer: termination, the emitted layer and the next state live in a single place, so the recursion is written once instead of re-derived in every builder.
Generation is separated from consumption, so the structure is produced on demand and callers can take what they need (take(n), limit, early exit, streaming sink) without materialising the rest.
Finite and infinite data are handled uniformly: the same scheme yields a ten-element list, an endless stream or a lazily expanded tree; only the step function's stop condition differs.
The step function is pure and small, so it can be property-tested for the coalgebra law (one layer per seed) without ever constructing the whole structure.
It composes with its dual: unfold followed by fold is a hylomorphism, and the intermediate structure disappears when both phases are fused.
tradeoffs: Termination is a proof obligation, not a guarantee: the scheme has no built-in stop condition, so an unbounded step function produces an infinite structure that hangs an eager consumer or exhausts memory.

Laziness has a retention cost: a suspended generator closes over its seed and environment, and memoising lazy structures (Scala LazyList, sequence caches) retain every produced element as long as the head is held.
No structural sharing: unfolding rebuilds every layer it needs, so regenerating a slightly different structure costs a full re-traversal instead of a local edit.
Deeply recursive assembly overflows the stack in strict languages unless the unfold is trampolined or driven by an explicit stack, which is exactly the boilerplate the scheme was meant to remove.

Per-step closures, boxing and per-layer allocation make it slower than a hand-written loop with a pre-sized buffer, and a wrong seed invariant yields a well-typed structure of the wrong shape that only the consumer notices.

participants.responsibility: The initial state value that the structure is generated from; an immutable value threaded through the scheme and never mutated in place, so the unfold can be replayed.
Decides for one seed whether generation stops and, if not, which layer to emit and which seed comes next - the only place where the pattern's domain logic lives.
Repeatedly applies the step function and assembles the produced layers into the target structure, or hands them to a sink as they are produced, driven by the consumer.
The recursive type the seed is expanded into (list, stream, tree, graph, syntax tree); it fixes the shape of one layer, the laziness and the reachable extent.
Forces the structure (fold, take(n), iteration, callback) and therefore decides how much is actually generated and when generation stops.

use_cases: Iterative numeric sequences (Collatz-style state walks, fixed-point search): expand the seed until the step function reports completion and hand the caller a lazy stream.
Pagination and continuation tokens: unfold one page request from the previous token, emitting records until the service signals exhaustion.
Building trees and graphs from a compact specification: expand a grammar production, a directory manifest, a quadtree cell or a decision-tree split into its recursive structure.
Property-based testing: turn a generator state into a lazy stream of arbitrary values and let the framework take as many samples as the failing case needs.
Parsing and compilation: unfold a token stream into a syntax tree, or emit output frames from a continuation state without materialising the intermediate document.
Search and simulation: expand a planner or game state into a move tree bounded by an explicit depth budget (fuel), which is the practical form when the state space is not finite.

Haskell's base library ships the canonical list anamorphism as Data.List.unfoldr :: (b -> Maybe (a, b)) -> b -> [a], and the containers package ships unfoldTree :: (b -> (a, [b])) -> b -> Tree a for (potentially infinite) rose trees - production form of the seed-plus-coalgebra scheme.

Scala's standard library exposes LazyList.unfold(seed)(f: S => Option[(A, S)]) (and Iterator.unfold) as the lazy-stream producer: each step runs only when the consumer forces it, so take(n) on an endless unfold does exactly n steps.

Kotlin's standard library encodes the same coalgebra as generateSequence(seed, nextFunction): the sequence is evaluated lazily and ends when nextFunction returns null, with the seed overload replayable from the seed on every iteration.
avoid_when: An equivalent structure already exists: consume it with a fold, a map or plain iteration instead of regenerating it through an unfold.
The elements arrive from an external producer (file, socket, database cursor): that is a pull iterator or a stream, and modelling it as a seed only hides the real source and its error handling.
The structure is fixed and small: a literal, a comprehension or a loop with append is shorter, cheaper and easier to read.
Generation and consumption always happen together: express the pair as one fused pass (a fold with an accumulator, or the hylomorphism it forms) and skip the intermediate structure.
Termination depends on global invariants that cannot be expressed per seed: a loop with an explicit exit condition and a monitor is more honest than a step function smuggling a flag.
anti_patterns: Unfold without fuel: an unbounded step function plus an eager consumer (toList, collect, spread) turns one wrong stop condition into a hang or an out-of-memory error.
Materialising an infinite unfold to take a handful of elements, instead of taking lazily or bounding the scheme at its entry point.
Presenting an external input source as a pure seed, so a pull loop pretends to be a pure producer and transport errors are lost.
Rebuilding an entire structure to change one layer where a fold with context (paramorphism) or a zipper would edit in place.
Hand-rolled recursive builders that re-implement the scheme per call site, each with a subtly different stop rule that no test covers.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the one-step rule (what to emit) is separated from assembly and consumption (when and how much).
Duality: generation (coalgebra) and consumption (algebra) are independent, so one producer composes with any consumer, and the pair can be fused.
Productivity as a design obligation: a coinductive definition must deliver each next layer in finite time, which makes the stop condition a first-class part of the design rather than an afterthought.
Open/closed principle: new structures and generators arrive as new step functions without touching the scheme.
Lazy evaluation as an ownership boundary: whoever forces the structure pays for it, so cost stays with the caller who benefits.
best_practices: Always pair the step function with an explicit stop condition or a fuel parameter - never rely on the caller to bound an unfold.
Keep the step function pure: no I/O, no mutation of the incoming seed, the next state returned as a value.
Bound recursion structurally: prefer the language's generator or iterator primitive so stack depth does not grow with the size of the produced structure.
Generate lazily and materialise at the edge: take(n)/limit before collecting, and stream into the consumer instead of through a container.
Name the seed's invariant and enforce it in the seed and layer types, so a wrongly shaped structure is unrepresentable rather than merely untested.
Prefer a built-in unfold or generator primitive over a hand-written recursive builder; write the builder only when laziness, ownership or error reporting exceeds what the primitive expresses.
When the result is consumed immediately, fuse unfold with fold instead of allocating the intermediate structure.
sources: Meijer, Fokkinga & Paterson, Functional Programming with Bananas, Lenses, Envelopes and Barbed Wire (1991) - introduces the recursion-scheme zoo in which the anamorphism (unfold) is the dual of the catamorphism and the two compose into a hylomorphism.
Bird & de Moor, Algebra of Programming (1997) - unfolds as the coalgebraic counterpart of folds, with the algebra-of-programming treatment of recursive definitions.

Gibbons & Jones, The Under-Appreciated Unfold (ICFP 1998) - argues unfolds are historically under-used versus folds and derives breadth-first traversal as an unfold: https://doi.org/10.1145/291251.289455
http://blog.dmitryleskov.com/programming/scala/stream-hygiene-i-avoiding-memory-leaks/ - documented misuse case: memoised lazy sequences retaining their realised spine
